concepts.title: DNA as the Genetic Material
concepts.definition: Three classic experiments crowned DNA as the hereditary molecule: Griffith's 1928 heat-killed smooth pneumococci passed a 'transforming principle' to harmless rough cells, Avery, MacLeod and McCarty wiped the principle out only with DNase, and Hershey and Chase watched radioactive phosphorus - not sulfur-labelled protein - ride into E. coli inside T2 phages.
concepts.key_idea: Whoever destroys DNA destroys the transforming ability, and only the phage's DNA enters the host - so DNA, not protein, carries heredity.
question_patterns: describe Griffith's transformation experiment with live smooth heat-killed smooth and rough strains of pneumococcus
which enzyme treated extract failed to transform rough bacteria in the Avery MacLeod McCarty experiment and why does that settle the case
why did Hershey and Chase label one phage batch with 32P and another with 35S
in the blender experiment where did the 35S and 32P radioactivity appear after centrifugation
who first isolated nuclein and from which cells
why are proteins an unlikely candidate for the genetic material despite their variety

solution_steps.explain: A heat-killed virulent strain converted live harmless cells into killers - something was transferred.
Protease and RNase extracts still transformed; only DNase stopped it, fingerpointing DNA.
32P-labelled DNA entered the pellet of bacteria while 35S-labelled protein stayed in the supernatant.

worked_examples.q: Who observed the transforming principle in 1928: Griffith or Hershey?

concepts.title: Gene Packaging in Prokaryotes and Eukaryotes
concepts.definition: Bacteria squeeze one circular chromosome into a nucleoid by negative supercoiling helped by histone-like proteins, while eukaryotes wind linear DNA around histone octamers of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4 into beads-on-string nucleosomes with a single H1 holding the linker, then coil 10 nm fibres through 30 nm and 300 nm stages to 700 nm metaphase chromosomes.
concepts.key_idea: Supercoiling packs the bacterial loop; histone spools and progressive folding tuck metres of eukaryotic DNA into a nucleus.
question_patterns: how does supercoiling compress the bacterial nucleoid and which direction does most bacterial DNA twist
name the histones forming the core octamer and the histone that binds linker DNA
how many base pairs of DNA wrap around one nucleosome and how many base pairs separate successive beads
trace the packaging ladder from the 2 nm double helix to the 700 nm metaphase chromosome
what are split genes - define introns and exons with the beta globin example
differentiate nuclear genome from organellar genome with reference to inheritance

solution_steps.explain: Prokaryotes: circular double-stranded DNA plus plasmids; eukaryotes: linear chromosomes inside a nucleus.
Nucleosome beads carry 146 bp of DNA on a histone octamer; linker DNA of about 200 bp per repeat separates them.
Beads fold to 30 nm fibres, loop on scaffolds to 300 nm, and condense maximally to 700 nm at metaphase.

worked_examples.q: DNA wound around histone octamers forms structures called what?

concepts.title: Genome Size Units and the Coding Fraction
concepts.definition: Genome sizes run from a few thousand bases in viruses to billions in mammals, and the reading convention chains them - a thousand base pairs make one kilobase and a thousand kilobases one megabase; the three-billion-base human genome carries over twenty thousand protein-coding genes that fill only about two percent of it, the rest being repetitive and other non-coding DNA.
concepts.key_idea: Divide bases by a thousand for kilobases and again for megabases; multiply the megabase total by the coding percent to size the gene share.
question_patterns: convert 3 billion base pairs of the human genome into kilobases and megabases
the human genome measures about 3000 megabases - how many base pairs is that
protein-coding genes occupy about 2 percent of a 3000 megabase genome - how many megabases carry genes
compare the genome size ranges of bacteria viruses and mammals on the base-pair scale
why do eukaryotic genomes carry far more non-coding DNA than prokaryotic ones
what are tandem repeats and where do they sit in the genome

solution_steps.explain: One thousand base pairs make one kilobase.
Another thousand-fold step gives megabases.
Coding regions take roughly two percent of the whole.

worked_examples.q: How many bases make one kilobase?

concepts.title: Semi-Conservative Replication Machinery
concepts.definition: Each daughter duplex keeps one parental strand and gains one new complement - the semi-conservative rule that Messelson and Stahl proved with heavy nitrogen and caesium chloride gradients; helicase unzips the fork, primase lays 10-12 nucleotide RNA primers, DNA polymerase III extends only 5' to 3', the lagging side is built in 1000-2000 nucleotide Okazaki pieces, polymerase I swaps primers for DNA, and ligase seals the nicks.
concepts.key_idea: One old strand plus one new strand per duplex, a continuous leading side and a discontinuous lagging side make replication semi-discontinuous.
question_patterns: describe the Messelson and Stahl experiment with 15N and 14N and the band positions after generations I and II
why does DNA polymerase III need an RNA primer while RNA polymerase does not
differentiate the leading strand from the lagging strand with reference to Okazaki fragments
which enzyme removes the RNA primers and which seals the gaps between fragments
what do helicase topoisomerase and SSB proteins each contribute at the replication fork
why is bacterial replication bidirectional and how many origins does each eukaryotic chromosome hold

solution_steps.explain: Initiator proteins and helicase separate strands from the origin; SSB proteins hold them apart while topoisomerase relieves the twist.
Primase lays short RNA primers; polymerase III adds dNTPs only onto a 3'OH, so synthesis runs 5' to 3'.
Okazaki fragments arise; polymerase I replaces each primer with DNA and ligase welds the fragments.

worked_examples.q: Who proved replication semi-conservative with heavy nitrogen: Meselson and Stahl, or Griffith?

concepts.title: Bacterial Division Timing and Culture Growth
concepts.definition: E. coli doubles every twenty minutes, so the generation count of an experiment is simply the elapsed minutes divided by twenty, and the culture size follows a doubling ladder from the starting cells.
concepts.key_idea: Divide the minutes by twenty for generations, then double the starter culture once per generation.
concepts.textbook_ref: kebt107.txt section 7.3.1 (E. coli divides after every 20 minutes)
question_patterns: how many generations does an E. coli culture complete in 2 hours of growth
a culture started with 3 cells and grew for 100 minutes - how many generations elapsed and how many cells stand at the end
Messelson and Stahl sampled after two rounds of division - how many minutes of growth does that represent
why did the two-band pattern of the second generation support semi-conservative replication
starting from one heavy-labelled cell how many hybrid duplexes exist after one generation in light medium
how long must E. coli grow to run through five generations

solution_steps.explain: One E. coli generation takes twenty minutes.
Each generation doubles the cell number from the starters.

worked_examples.q: How many minutes does E. coli need to divide: twenty or sixty?

concepts.title: Genetic Code Triplet Arithmetic
concepts.definition: Gamow's counting settled the code's design: one base gives only four options and a pair sixteen - too few for twenty amino acids - but a three-base code offers sixty-four codons; sixty-one of them specify amino acids, the remaining three are stops, AUG doubles as the start signal, and Nirenberg's poly-U decoded the first word, UUU for phenylalanine.
concepts.key_idea: Four raised to the codon length counts the code; subtract the three stops for the sense codons.
question_patterns: why must a codon contain three bases - show the counting for one two and three base codes
how many of the 64 codons code for amino acids and which three signal termination
which codon starts translation and which amino acid does it carry - state its dual role
what did the poly-U experiment of Nirenberg and Matthaei establish
explain degeneracy of the genetic code and name the two amino acids with single codons
why is the code called unambiguous and universal despite mitochondrial exceptions

solution_steps.explain: Four bases taken three at a time give four cubed combinations.
UAA, UAG and UGA terminate translation instead of coding.
Each amino acid costs three bases and the stop adds three more.

worked_examples.q: How many codons does the genetic code hold in total?

concepts.title: Transcription, mRNA Processing and Translation
concepts.definition: RNA polymerase reads a promoter with its Pribnow box, unwinds about seventeen base pairs and strings ribonucleotides at roughly forty per second until a terminator - with sigma leaving after initiation and rho sometimes ending the run; eukaryotic transcripts then gain a methyl-G cap and a poly-A tail and lose their introns by splicing, before ribosomes translate the message codon by codon from charged tRNAs until a release factor meets a stop codon.
concepts.key_idea: Copy only the gene into RNA, dress and trim the eukaryotic transcript, then let tRNAs and the wobble rule translate it at the ribosome.
question_patterns: list the three steps of transcription and state the role of the sigma factor and the Pribnow box
which RNA polymerase transcribes hnRNA in eukaryotes and which RNAs do polymerases I and III make
name the three post-transcriptional modifications of eukaryotic pre-mRNA and the purpose of each
differentiate the coding strand from the template strand of a transcription unit
describe charging of tRNA by aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase and the wobble pairing at the third codon base
how does a release factor end translation and what is a polyribosome
how long an RNA does bacterial polymerase build in one minute at 37 degrees celsius

solution_steps.explain: Sigma-guided polymerase binds upstream, melts the TATAAT region and starts RNA without a primer.
The transcription bubble advances at about 40 nucleotides per second until rho-dependent or independent termination.
Cap, splice and poly-adenylate in eukaryotes; then initiation, elongation and termination build the polypeptide in the ribosome's A, P and E sites.

worked_examples.q: Roughly how many nucleotides per second does RNA polymerase string: forty or four?

concepts.title: Gene Mutation and DNA Repair Arithmetic
concepts.definition: Mutations come as additions, deletions and substitutions - purine-for-purine changes are transitions while purine-for-pyrimidine swaps are transversions, and tautomeric shifts or base analogs like 5-bromouracil sneak such swaps past replication; cells answer with base excision repair through glycosylase-made AP sites, nucleotide excision repair that cuts out UV-induced T-T dimers by clipping upstream and downstream, and mismatch repair led by Mut proteins.
concepts.key_idea: Add the two cut distances around a lesion to size the patch that excision repair must refill.
question_patterns: NER clips eight nucleotides upstream and four downstream of a T-T dimer - how many nucleotides are excised in all
differentiate transition and transversion mutations with one base change example of each
how does a rare enol tautomer of guanine turn a G-C pair into an A-T pair over two replications
why does 5-bromouracil pair with adenine in its keto form but with guanine in its enol form
which enzyme creates the AP site in base excision repair and which enzymes fill and seal it
name the Mut proteins of mismatch repair and state how far from the mismatch the cut falls
which mutation class - addition deletion or substitution - disrupts the whole reading frame and why

solution_steps.explain: The Uvr system nicks a fixed distance upstream of the damage.
A shorter nick lands downstream of the damage.
The removed patch spans both sides of the lesion.

worked_examples.q: A purine-for-purine substitution is called a what: transition or transversion?

solution_template.explain: Each position independently takes four bases.
